Far East Organization to preview freehold project The Serra Residences on Oct 2
article:
Far East Organization will preview The Serra Residences , a 133-unit development within the Novena residential enclave, on Oct 2. Sales bookings for the freehold project will commence on Oct 16.

Located along Bassein Road in District 11, The Serra Residences comprises a single 28-storey residential tower. Unit types on levels four to 16 include two-bedroom with study units ranging from 710 to 721 sq ft, three-bedroom units of 764 to 904 sq ft, and four-bedroom units measuring 958 sq ft.

The development also features The Summit , which occupies levels 18 to 28 and comprises larger-format four-bedroom units ranging from 1,216 to 1,528 sq ft, five-bedroom premium units measuring 1,755 sq ft, and two penthouses spanning 2,648 and 2,669 sq ft.

Search for the latest New Launches , to find out the transaction prices and available units

The Serra Residences occupies the plot of the former Pastoral View condo. In 2010, Far East Organization acquired the site through a collective sale, together with the adjoining plot, for a total of $122 million. The two freehold sites have a combined land area of 51,396 sq ft.

“When we brought the former Pastoral View and its neighbouring plot together, we saw an opportunity to create something seldom found in the city — an intimate community of 133 homes with the facilities of a much larger development,” said Shaw Lay See, chief operating officer of Far East Organization’s Sales and Leasing Group.

According to the developer, The Serra Residences is situated within an established neighbourhood that is evolving into a “lifestyle and healthcare precinct”. It is next to the integrated healthcare hub HealthCity Novena and within a four- to nine-minute drive of retail and dining amenities at Novena Square , United Square and Newton Food Centre.

The development is also an eight-minute walk from Novena MRT Station. Schools within a 2km radius include St. Joseph’s Institution Junior, Anglo-Chinese School (Barker Road and Junior), and Hong Wen School.

The Serra Residences is one of only two freehold launches in the Core Central Region (CCR) in 2026, according to Huttons Asia CEO Mark Yip. “It offers buyers an opportunity to own a freehold non-landed home in the CCR for both wealth preservation and legacy planning,” he said.

Of the 4,000 new private non-landed homes launched in the region in the first two quarters of this year, only 287, or 7%, are freehold, Yip added.

As healthcare becomes increasingly important for Singapore’s ageing population, continued expansion of HealthCity Novena will likely be a significant driver for the surrounding precinct, ERA Singapore CEO Marcus Chu notes.

“Against this backdrop, The Serra Residences offers buyers an opportunity to be part of a neighbourhood with well-established fundamentals and long-term potential,” he remarked.

Kelvin Fong, CEO of PropNex, expects the project to garner interest from both owner-occupiers looking for a legacy home, as well as investors.

“With a number of recent CCR launches achieving average prices above $3,000 psf, the market has demonstrated that buyers are willing to transact at these levels for well-located prime projects,” he noted.

The Serra Residences is expected to receive its temporary occupation permit in 4Q2030.

Upon completion, SRI managing partner Ken Low expects the development to benefit from Novena’s “established and resilient” rental market, supported by demand from healthcare professionals and families.

Designed by P&T Consultants, The Serra Residences features mountain-inspired architecture, with vertical facade lines and stone and timber elements.

Kingsley Ng, architect and director at P&T Consultants, said: “Like natural formations shaped over time, the tower is sculpted into layered voids that reveal elevated green terraces and communal spaces for residents to gather, retreat and connect with nature.”

Facilities at the development are spread across the second, third and 17th storeys. They include a tennis court, 50m lap pool, kids’ pool, pet park, sauna, and social and retreat lounges.

title: From snow rooms to sound baths: Inside Morrow’s approach to longevity
article:
Stepping into a room chilled to sub-zero temperatures might not be the most conventional way to pursue a longer, healthier life.

Yet at Morrow, a new integrated longevity destination at 10 Coleman Street, extreme temperatures are part of the experience. Its snow room is kept between -5°C and -10°C, while a whole-body cryotherapy chamber takes the cold considerably further, plunging to -110°C for brief, supervised sessions.

They are among a wide range of recovery, movement, nutrition and health offerings brought together at Morrow, which occupies more than 36,000 sq ft within the recently opened Longevity World mall.

The 80,000 sq ft wellness-dedicated mall is part of a mixed-use development that includes five-star Grand Park City Hall .

The site is in the Civic District, a short walk from City Hall MRT Station and close to malls such as Funan , Capitol Singapore and Raffles City Shopping Centre , as well as landmarks including the National Gallery Singapore and Old Hill Street Police Station.

Morrow was founded by entrepreneur Allen Law, who is also principal at Seveno Capital, a venture capital fund that invests in health, wellness and longevity-related businesses. Law is also founder of luxury hotel operator Park Hotel Group, whose portfolio includes Grand Park City Hall.

Longevity World is the larger umbrella encompassing Morrow and Morrow Medical.

The wellness hub is envisioned as an ecosystem of complementary health and wellness offerings spanning preventive medicine, fitness, recovery, nutrition, beauty and lifestyle concepts. More operators are expected to join the mix, including traditional Chinese medicine providers.

Another concept within the Longevity World ecosystem is Glow Food, a 100% plant-based food hall comprising six concepts. Its offerings range from Taiwanese-style bento boxes and build-your-own salads to noodles, burrito wraps, sandwiches and smoothies.

The salad selection follows five colour groups — red, green, yellow, black and white — while protein choices include chickpeas, tempeh and lentils. The emphasis is largely on whole foods rather than mock meats and heavily processed meat alternatives.

From health data to action

The wellness-focused Morrow forms the heart of the experience. Its facilities span movement and exercise, thermal experiences, recovery treatments and nutrition, with Morrow Medical located one floor above.

Jaclyn Chan, general manager at Morrow, says the idea is not simply to assemble a collection of novel wellness facilities.

“If you do a health test and get your results but don’t do anything about them, then yes, you’re more informed, but it doesn’t change your health,” she says.

Morrow therefore aims to bridge the gap between knowing and doing. Its Morrow Insights assessment, conducted by Morrow Medical, establishes a health baseline through a series of tests.

These include a VO₂ max test to measure how efficiently the body uses oxygen during exercise, and a DEXA scan, which measures bone density and provides a breakdown of body composition, including muscle, body fat and visceral fat around the organs.

Strength and power assessments examine areas such as grip strength, jumping ability and potential imbalances between the left and right sides of the body.

The assessment also includes spirometry to measure lung function, alongside blood tests, vital signs and an evaluation of psychological well-being. For those unable to undertake a full VO₂ max test, a less strenuous option is available.

The results can inform how a member exercises and which areas require greater attention.

Chan gives the example of someone who might regularly choose strength classes when their results suggest that cardiovascular fitness or another area warrants more focus.

This feeds into Morrow’s broader objective of narrowing the gap between lifespan — how long someone lives — and healthspan, or the period of life spent in good health.

“People are living longer now,” she says. “Yes, we want to increase lifespan, but your healthspan needs to catch up.”

Turning up the temperature — then dropping it

One of the more memorable stops on my tour was Morrow’s Renewal Zone, where contrast therapy takes centre stage.

There are hot immersion pools kept between 40°C and 42°C, as well as cold plunges ranging from 6°C to 15°C. Members can alternate between hot and cold environments, with a sauna, steam room and experiential shower rounding out the thermal facilities.

Then there is the snow room.

Kept between -5°C and -10°C, the dry room offers a less extreme cold environment than Morrow’s whole-body cryotherapy chamber. The latter reaches -110°C, with sessions typically lasting just two to three minutes.

Other recovery modalities include hyperbaric oxygen therapy and red-light therapy. Chan says the team looked at the clinical research available when deciding which equipment and treatments to introduce.

Technology also features prominently in Morrow’s spacious gym. The gym includes Technogym Biostrength, an AI-enabled digital strength circuit that takes into account a user’s range of motion before guiding the workout. The system can adjust settings, guide tempo, record performance and recommend changes based on how the user performs.

Workout data can also be integrated into the Morrow app to track progress over time.

Seeing the equipment adjust to the individual was one of the more interesting parts of the tour, particularly compared with conventional strength machines where users typically determine their own settings, resistance and progression.

Whole foods at Folium

Before exploring the rest of Morrow, we had lunch at Folium, its wholefoods restaurant. Morrow describes its approach as “culinary medicine”, combining plant-forward ingredients and nutritional science with an emphasis on whole foods.

Folium means ‘leaf’ in Latin. The kitchen uses little salt, oil and sauces, to let the flavours of the ingredients come through, says Chan.

The Coastal Snapper Tacos paired fish with kohlrabi, purple cabbage and lime crema on chapati , while the Miso Salmon came with brown rice, zucchini, beetroot and button mushrooms — a medley of colours. The Cauliflower Steak, served with quinoa and baby spinach, was also surprisingly substantial. Portions across the meal were generous and filling.

Of the desserts, the Chocolate H2O Rock, was a surprise. Made from 100% dark chocolate and water, I expected it to be intensely bitter. Instead, it was slightly sweet and reminded me of chocolate ice cream, only without the creaminess. The other dessert was a Honey Basque Cheesecake.

The meal also included a Vital Sip of ginger, apple cider vinegar, lemon and honey, and a Vanilla Sour made with kombucha, vanilla, lemon and egg white.

Slowing down with sound

After touring the facilities, we ended our visit with a yoga and sound therapy session — a considerably less high-tech experience than the gym downstairs, for members to unplug.

The session began with breathing exercises and gentle stretches. At one point, while I was lying face-down, the instructor placed a singing bowl directly on my back and gently struck it with a mallet.

Rather than simply hearing the resulting tone, I could feel the vibrations through my body, making the sound a physical sensation as well as an audible one.

Yoga made up roughly a third of the session, with the remaining two-thirds devoted to sound therapy.

For this, yoga blocks and towels were arranged to support my body, including beneath my knees and elbows, while a small towel covered my eyes. The instructor then used singing bowls, chimes and a gong to produce a succession of sounds as I lay still and focused on my breathing.

With my eyes covered, changes in pitch, vibration and the direction of the sounds became more noticeable. For most of the session, there was little required of me beyond lying still, breathing and listening.

That slower pace ties back to Chan’s view of longevity as something broader than medical testing and exercise.

“[For many of us in Singapore,] we’re constantly being pulled in multiple directions,” she says. “Sometimes our bodies break down, and it’s not because they haven’t been giving us signals. We just don’t pause to listen.”

The snow room, cryotherapy chamber and AI-enabled gym equipment are among Morrow’s more attention-grabbing features, while Folium and the sound therapy session show other facets of its well-rounded approach.

What links them is Morrow’s attempt to bring health assessment, exercise, recovery, nutrition and mental well-being into the same place.

Without that common thread, the risk is that Morrow just becomes “a bunch of cool things under one roof”, as Chan puts it.

Whether visitors make use of that entire ecosystem or gravitate towards individual parts of it will depend on their needs.

My visit offered only a snapshot — a tour of the facilities, lunch at Folium and one yoga and sound therapy session — but it provided a look at how Morrow is bringing several aspects of the increasingly broad longevity space together under one roof.

title: M&G Real Estate sells Tokyo residential tower
article:
M&G Real Estate has sold Frontier Shinjuku Tower, a 24-storey building in Tokyo, Japan for an undisclosed sum.

According to Mingtiandi, the building was sold to flexible living provider Dash Living for JPY38 billion (about $309 million).

Frontier Shinjuku Tower has 298 residential apartments, alongside retail and office space. M&G had purchased the tower in January 2024 for JPY30 billion.

The real estate investment manager carried out enhancements to the building, including upgrading shared amenities and repurposing underutilised space. It also introduced sustainability initiatives, with the development achieving a CASBEE S rating, the highest rank under Japan’s green building certification.

The sale of Frontier Shinjuku Tower follows a 23% increase in the building’s net operating income, said M&G in a Sept 28 release. The transaction was also completed 15 months ahead of M&G’s original business plan.

“Frontier Shinjuku Tower presented an opportunity to acquire a high-quality asset and create additional value through targeted improvements and active management,” said Jing Dong Lai, CEO and chief investment officer of M&G Real Estate Asia.

“The strong income growth achieved during our ownership, combined with an accelerated sale, demonstrates how local market expertise and disciplined execution can deliver attractive outcomes for investors,” he added.

title: URA launches tender for East Coast Road GLS site; opens applications for Serangoon North View plot
article:
A residential Government Land Sale (GLS) site at East Coast Road has been launched for sale by tender under the 2H2026 GLS Programme. The 99-year leasehold site spans 94,776 sq ft and can yield about 85 homes, said URA in a Sept 29 release.

URA also announced that a Reserve List site at Serangoon North View is available for application. The 217,592 sq ft, 99-year leasehold plot can yield around 235 residential units.

Smaller East Coast Road plot to draw healthy interest

The East Coast Road site is the second-smallest GLS plot ever offered in terms of dwelling units, according to Mark Yip, CEO of Huttons Asia. The smallest was a site at Chong Kuo Road awarded in February 2018, which later became the 84-unit The Essence .

An open drain cuts through the East Coast Road site, separating it into two plots, observed Wong Siew Ying, head of research and content at PropNex.

Based on the tender details, one of these could be developed into long-stay serviced apartments. "There is also the option to develop the land parcel as one single development over both plots, or as two separate developments on each plot," she added.

Wong also pointed out that a minimum average unit size of 100 sq m (1,076 sq ft) is stipulated for the plot. "The future project built on this site will likely offer larger, family-oriented homes and may appeal to right-sizers from landed housing in the area," she said.

Marcus Chu, CEO of ERA Singapore, believes the site will appeal to developers targeting smaller developments. Earlier this month, the tender for a nearby GLS site at New Upper Changi Road was awarded to a consortium comprising CapitaLand Development, UOL Group and UOL subsidiary Singapore Land Group.

The consortium’s offer of $1.43 billion, $1,537 psf per plot ratio (psf ppr), topped three other bids for the site, which can accommodate about 1,010 homes.

In comparison, the significantly smaller East Coast Road site would have lower capital investment and execution risks, said Chu. “Well-located boutique sites enable developers to manage construction, pricing and sales risks more effectively while meeting owner-occupiers’ demand,” he continued.

Chu expects the East Coast Road site to attract wide developer interest, given its strong locational attributes. The plot is within walking distance of the Siglap MRT Station on the Thomson-East Coast Line, while also being near lifestyle and retail offerings at Siglap Centre and Siglap V .

In addition, it is close to several schools, including Opera Estate Primary School, Ngee Ann Primary School, CHIJ Katong Convent, St. Patrick’s School, Victoria School, and Victoria Junior College.

Housing demand in the Bedok Planning Area, where the East Coast Road site is located, remains resilient, Chu adds. In April, the 515-unit Vela Bay in Bayshore saw 72% of units taken up at an average price of $2,886 psf on launch day.

Given these factors, he expects the East Coast Road site to attract over five bidders, with a top bid of around $1,400 psf ppr. “Developers' ongoing interest in well-positioned and established residential estates shows confidence that carefully planned projects in established neighbourhoods remain some of the most resilient options in Singapore’s residential market,” he remarked.

Huttons’ Yip believes the site could garner up to five bids, with the highest bid ranging between $1,100 and $1,300 psf ppr.

Meanwhile, PropNex's Wong expects "healthy but selective interest" from developers. She predicts three to five offers for the site, with a top bid ranging from $1,550 to $1,650 psf ppr.

The tender for the East Coast Road site will close at noon on Dec 3.

Serangoon North View site unlikely to be triggered for sale

The Serangoon North View plot is adjacent to the Serangoon North Avenue 1 GLS site (now the 613-unit The Garden Residences ) that was awarded in August 2017 at $965 psf ppr, according to Wong. "While not particularly close to an MRT station presently, the future Serangoon North station (CR9) on the Cross Island Line, which is targeted to open in 2030, is roughly 700m away from the site," she added.

However, Wong does not expect developers to trigger the plot for sale, given upcoming private housing supply nearby. Two GLS sites at Chuan Grove awarded last year will yield over 1,000 new units in total.

Additionally, a Reserve List site at Chuan Grove, which can offer around 935 units, will be made available in October.

title: GBP20 mil duplex penthouse launched for sale at London’s Southbank Place
article:
A four-bedroom duplex penthouse at Southbank Place in London has been launched for sale at GBP20 million ($33.9 million).

The 3,800 sq ft home occupies the 12th and 13th floors of Seven, the final building in the GBP1 billion ($1.69 billion) Southbank Place development.

Called the Albion Nord Penthouse, it comes with about 900 sq ft of private wraparound terrace and is designed by British interior design studio Albion Nord, which was also engaged for the interior architecture of Seven.

Looking to invest in overseas properties ? Explore projects available for sale around the world

Full-height windows at the unit offer views across London, including the Houses of Parliament, London Eye and River Thames.

Southbank Place is a 5.25-acre (2.12ha, or 228,690 sq ft) development surrounding the Shell Tower and is being developed by Braeburn Estates, a joint venture between Qatari Diar and Canary Wharf Group.

Bespoke furniture and commissioned artwork

The interiors retain exposed travertine and concrete elements, alongside darker timbers, polished plaster and fabrics including mohair and shearling.

Among the bespoke pieces is a hand-blown glass pendant by Carricks in the living area. A woven rug takes its design from the flow of the River Thames, while a handcrafted desk by Stride & Co and a dining table by Albion Nord feature angular forms that reference the architecture of the penthouse and building.

The home also contains commissioned works by artists including Anne Griffiths, Philip Maltman, Karl Blossfeldt, Ines Fernandes de Crodova and Danielle Creenaune. Photography of cityscapes by Alexsandr Babarikin is displayed throughout the penthouse.

“The detailing is refined, the material choice is varied, and the furniture is a thoughtful blend of old and new,” says Ben Johnson, director at Albion Nord. “The carefully sourced antiques sit comfortably alongside bespoke furniture and lighting creations that have been designed especially for the space.”

Two floors overlooking London

On the lower floor, a central gallery leads to the open-plan living and dining areas and kitchen. It also contains a private study, guest bedroom suite with its own balcony, utility room and powder room.

Upstairs, a glazed mezzanine overlooks the main living space. The principal bedroom suite has an en suite bathroom with a fluted stone wall, freestanding bath, separate shower and twin sinks, as well as two walk-in dressing rooms.

Two additional guest bedroom suites complete the upper floor.

All four bedrooms in the duplex unit have bespoke wall-to-wall headboards, commissioned artwork and individually selected soft furnishings.

Residents have direct lift access to Southbank Place’s basement health club, which includes a 25m swimming pool, steam and sauna rooms, gym, treatment rooms, relaxation pods and a hair and beauty studio.

Southbank Place is connected to Waterloo Station and located near the Royal Festival Hall and the Southbank Centre arts centre, while the National Theatre and The Old Vic are within walking distance.

title: DBS, OCBC or UOB — Which Singapore Bank Stock Actually Made You the Most Money?
article:
DBS Group Holdings
(SGX: D05),
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, and
United Overseas Bank
(SGX: U11), or UOB, have been favourites among
income investors
.
Over the past decade, the three banks have rewarded their shareholders through both rising share prices and dividends.
But looking at the share price alone misses the whole picture.
This article looks at which one would have made you the most money if you had invested S$10,000 in each bank 10 years ago.
The S$10,000 Test
For a fair comparison, we assume S$10,000 was invested in each bank on 23 September 2016 and held until 23 September 2026.
We include both share-price appreciation and all dividends received over the period.
DBS’s 2024 one-for-10 bonus issue is also reflected in the share count.
Brokerage fees and taxes are excluded.

The winner is clear.
A S$10,000 investment in DBS would have grown to roughly S$69,200, including dividends.
The same amount invested in OCBC would be worth about S$44,400, while UOB would have grown to around S$29,900.
What Drove the Difference?
DBS delivered the strongest earnings growth, with net profit rising from S$4.2 billion in 2016 to S$10.9 billion in 2025, while ROE improved from 10.1% to 16.2%.
OCBC’s net profit more than doubled from S$3.5 billion to S$7.4 billion over the same period, supported by its banking, wealth management and insurance businesses.
UOB’s net profit rose from S$3.1 billion in 2016 to S$4.7 billion in 2025, an increase of 52%. Its slower earnings growth relative to DBS and OCBC partly explains its more modest share-price appreciation over the decade.
The Dividend Difference
Dividends were also an important part of the return for all three banks.

DBS produced the most dividend income in dollar terms, but its large capital gains meant dividends accounted for around one-fifth of its overall gain.
For UOB, dividends contributed more than one-third of the total gain.
This shows why looking only at a share price chart can understate the returns generated by mature dividend stocks.
What If You Reinvested Every Dividend?
Taking dividends as cash provides income today, but reinvesting gives investors more investment opportunities.
With reinvestment, each dividend would buy additional shares, which then generate their own dividends.
Over time, this creates a
compounding effect
and increases the final portfolio value.
The impact is particularly powerful when dividend growth is paired with rising share prices since those additional shares will now also participate in future capital gains.
The Pandemic Put Bank Dividends to the Test
COVID-19 also showed that the banks’ dividends do not depend on earnings alone.
During the pandemic back in 2020, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) capped Singapore banks’ dividends at 60% of their 2019 levels to preserve capital.
As a result, the three banks reduced their payouts despite remaining profitable.
The restrictions were lifted in 2021 and dividends subsequently recovered – a reason why historical dividend growth should not simply be extrapolated in a straight line.
Dividend Growth Matters Too
For long-term shareholders, growing dividends can increase the income earned on the original investment.
This is known as the yield on cost.
Someone who bought the shares at much lower prices in 2016 could now be receiving a much higher yield on their original S$10,000 than the dividend yield we see today.
DBS gets the spotlight here as its dividends per share has increased substantially over the decade together with stronger earnings and capital generation.
Valuation Matters More Than It Seems
Historical returns are affected by not only how quickly a company grows but also the price investors are willing to pay.
If earnings rise while the market is also willing to assign a higher valuation to those earnings, shareholders benefit from both growth and valuation expansion.
Again, DBS enjoyed both over the 10 years.
However, historical winners do not automatically make the best investment today.
Future returns will still depend on many factors like today’s valuation, earnings growth, and dividend sustainability.

Over this particular 10-year period,
DBS
was the clear winner.
It produced both the largest capital gain and the most dividend income, turning S$10,000 into almost S$70,000.
OCBC came in second with about S$44,400, while UOB finished third at around S$30,000.
But this comparison also highlights something more important than just identifying the historical winner.
What Can Investors Learn From the Three-Bank Experiment?
The first takeaway is simple:
dividends matter
.
Share-price gains are only part of the return, and dividends can make a meaningful difference over time.
Starting valuation matters too because paying a lower price gives investors more room for future returns.
Dividend growth can steadily lift income and yield on cost, but it ultimately depends on a strong underlying business.
And lastly, things change, so the bank that looked the most attractive 10 years ago may not offer the best value today.

The S$10,000 test shows why investors should look beyond share prices and include dividends when measuring returns.

title: Dividend Trap or Bargain? How to Tell When a High Yield Is Misleading
article:
Every income investor loves a bargain.
When a familiar blue-chip real estate investment trust (REIT) drops towards its 52-week low, pushing its trailing dividend yield above 6%, the impulse to click “buy” can be almost overwhelming.
On paper, the maths looks enticing.
But in dividend investing, superficial screening is one of the quickest ways to walk into a
yield trap
.
Here are the key red flags to evaluate to make sure you are buying a sturdy compounder rather than a crumbling trap.
Is the Yield High Only Because the Price Crashed?
A dividend yield is a mathematical fraction: distribution per unit (DPU) divided by unit price.
Yield rises in two ways: either the REIT grows its underlying rental income, or the market sells off the REIT, driving down the unit price while the trailing DPU has yet to reflect any future cuts.
When a REIT sits near its 52-week low, the second scenario is usually at play.
Consider
Landmark REIT
(SGX: D5IU), or what was formerly known as Lippo Malls Indonesia Retail Trust (LMIRT), as an extreme cautionary case study.
As severe currency depreciation, high debt refinancing costs, and falling asset valuations pushed its unit price down by over 80% in recent years, headline trailing yield looked deceptively attractive – right before distributions were completely halted to preserve liquidity.
If a REIT’s past 12-month DPU gives you a 6.5% trailing yield today, but its forward income is set to drop by 10% due to higher financing costs or tenant vacancies, that 6.5% yield is a mirage.
Unmasking the DPU Trend
When evaluating any dividend payer, direction matters far more than snapshot magnitude.
A REIT yielding 5% with a consistent three-year track record of growing DPU is healthier than a REIT yielding 7% with shrinking distributions.
Look beyond the single annualised percentage and check whether the latest 1H or 2H DPU is growing organically or sliding year on year (YoY).
Watch out for distributions padded by one-off divestment gains or temporary top-ups.
Take
Mapletree Logistics Trust
(SGX: M44U), or MLT.
For the quarter ended 30 June 2026 (1QFY2026/2027), its DPU was S$0.01816, barely changed from S$0.01812 a year earlier.
A weaker Japanese yen, Korean won and Hong Kong dollar held back growth: without currency effects, gross revenue would have risen 2.0% instead of 0.8%.
Note, too, that S$0.00834 of that DPU, almost half, was paid as a capital distribution.
That is not a red flag on its own.
It made up a similar share a year earlier (S$0.00797), so it is a recurring part of MLT’s payout rather than a one-off top-up.
The lesson: read the distribution breakdown before deciding whether a payout is padded.
High Leverage and Refinancing Squeezes
Singapore REITs continue to navigate an
elevated interest rate
environment.
For highly leveraged REITs, older low-cost fixed debt is continually expiring and being refinanced at significantly higher rates.
Look closely at three balance sheet metrics:
Gearing ratio:
Is aggregate leverage hovering dangerously close to, or above, 40%?
Interest Coverage Ratio (ICR):
Is the ICR narrowing, leaving little margin for error?
Debt maturity profile:
How much debt matures over the next 12 to 18 months?
Suntec REIT
(SGX: T82U) shows why the balance sheet deserves a close look even when payouts are rising.
Its DPU jumped 24.8% YoY to S$0.03936 in 1H2026, helped by lower financing costs.
Yet its aggregate leverage climbed from 41.5% to 43.0% over the same six months.
Around S$810 million of borrowings, almost a fifth of its debt, falls due within 12 months.
Meanwhile, the share of debt on fixed rates slipped from about 65% to 57%.
That leaves distributions more exposed to rate changes.
Suntec estimates that a one-percentage-point rise in its financing cost would cut DPU by S$0.0177 a year.
Get Smart: Look for Deep Roots, Not Just High Sprouts
It is easy to see why investors get excited when a big-name REIT touches a 52-week low with a headline yield above 6%.
But a
high yield
on its own tells you nothing about the health of the underlying business.
Before committing your hard-earned capital, look past the trailing headline yield.
Inspect the core operational trajectory: is DPU growing organically, is the debt profile well laddered, and is management protecting unitholder value?
Just like choosing a plant for your garden, selecting income stocks requires looking beneath the surface.
You do not want a portfolio built on flimsy, shallow roots like
taugeh
– the moment economic winds shift or interest rates stay higher for longer, they wither fast.
Instead, you want investments structured like an oak tree: deeply rooted, structurally sound, and capable of weathering macroeconomic storms.
For long-term wealth accumulation, seek out businesses built on strong balance sheets, quality properties, and sustainable cash flows that can continue paying you steady dividends for decades to come.
Many Singapore stocks fall behind inflation, which means your money quietly loses strength over time. Dividend stocks have a very different track record. Some continued delivering 6% to 13% every year across the toughest market conditions.

title: 10 Things I Wish I Knew Before I Started Investing in Singapore
article:
Investing for the first time is intimidating.
With countless financial products, from stocks and
real estate investment trusts (REITs)
, to
exchange-traded funds (ETFs)
and bonds, new investors often get lost trying to find the “next big thing”.
Many investing mistakes are only obvious after money is lost.
Save yourself from expensive mistakes with these ten things that I wish I knew before I started investing:
1. Investing Is a Long Game
Short-term share price swings are usually noise.
Investment performance is driven by the underlying business’s ability to grow earnings, cash flow, and
dividends
.
The real win comes from staying invested in strong businesses long enough for compounding to work.
At a hypothetical 6% annual return, a 30-year investment of S$10,000 with dividends reinvested will give you about S$57,000.
By starting 10 years later, you will only have approximately S$32,000.
2. A Good Company Isn’t Always a Good Investment
A strong brand with competitive advantages does not eliminate valuation risk.
Overpaying for a great business can still produce disappointing results when much of the optimism has been priced in.
Checking metrics like price-to-earnings (P/E), price-to-book (P/B), and free cash flow helps assess whether the current price is reasonable.
3. High Dividend Yields Can Be Traps
High dividend yields are attractive.
However,
abnormally high yields
of 7% to 10% often hide red flags like falling share prices, high debt, or an unsustainable payout ratio.
Rather than obsessing over large payouts, look at what’s driving the dividends.
Focus on companies with steady cash flow, reasonable debt, and a reliable dividend history.
Regardless of economic conditions, Singapore’s three big banks,
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05),
United Overseas Bank Limited
(SGX: U11), or UOB, and
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, have never stopped paying dividends.
4. Dividend Reinvestment Is a Compounding Engine
Spending your dividends feels great.
But reinvesting them turns these payments into more shares without additional capital from you.
These shares not only pay more dividends in the future, but also increase your total returns with capital appreciation.
5. 10 Holdings Aren’t Automatically “Diversified”
Having a lot of different stocks does not automatically mean you are diversified.
Owning DBS, OCBC, and UOB gives you three tickers, but they are 100% concentrated in Singapore and the banking sector.
As banks and REITs offer substantial dividends, Singapore investors tend to have the bulk of their portfolios in these sectors, increasing concentration risk.
True diversification is owning quality assets across sectors, countries, business models, and asset types.
Consider a portfolio that includes a Singapore bank as a dividend anchor, a consumer defensive stock like
Sheng Siong Group Ltd
(SGX: OV8), a strong REIT like
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), and a US growth stock like
NVIDIA
(NASDAQ: NVDA).
6. Singapore Investors Don’t Have to Stay Local
Unlike the Singapore market, which offers dividends from mature businesses, the
US stock market
offers opportunities in high-growth listed companies that often do not have a local equivalent.
Your Singapore stocks can be your source of steady income, while investments in US stocks or global ETFs are your key to broad growth.
Be wary of currency risks and
tax considerations
when you invest overseas.
7. Market Crashes Are Features, Not Bugs
Market corrections are a normal part of investing.
Economic uncertainty, unexpected global events, and investor sentiment can all cause market fluctuations.
Look beyond share prices and examine metrics such as revenue and earnings growth, free cash flow, and balance-sheet strength to evaluate whether the investment thesis still holds.
8. Trading Too Often Destroys Compound Returns
Taking a quick 15% gain feels like winning.
After all, the profit is only guaranteed when it’s cashed out.
However,
trading
too often can cut long-term winners short and incur unnecessary transaction costs.
If prices keep climbing, you might have to buy back at a higher price or miss dividend payouts while waiting on the sidelines.
Sell based on deteriorating fundamentals or extreme overvaluation, not minor price spikes.
9. Your Behaviour Is Your Biggest Risk
Emotional investing is a trap.
When you chase surging stocks due to the fear of missing out (FOMO), panic-sell during market fluctuations, or blindly follow social media and “insider” tips, you can lose more than any market crash would cost you.
Establish a structured, rule-based process such as clear criteria for when you buy and sell to protect your capital.
10. Starting Early Beats Starting Perfectly
Small, consistent investments beat sitting on cash as you wait for the “perfect” stock or for that market bottom that might never come.
You might have thought OCBC hit its peak when it traded at approximately S$20 per share in January 2026 and wanted to wait for a correction.
However, its shares have continued to climb and traded at S$32.01 as of 25 September 2026.
Those who waited on the sidelines for a correction that didn’t come missed a 60% share price gain and a total of S$1.05 per share in dividends.
Instead of waiting, start with a small investment of S$1,000 to S$5,000 in quality companies.
Thereafter, use
dollar-cost averaging
to invest regularly and let time do the heavy lifting.
Checklist Before Buying A Stock
Before buying a stock, take time and go through these four points:
Business:
Do I understand how this company makes money?
Health:
Is debt manageable and backed by positive free cash flow? Are dividends sustainable?
Valuation:
Is the P/E or P/B ratio reasonable relative to its historical average? Is the share price too high or a steal?
Portfolio:
Where does this holding fit in my existing portfolio? Will it increase concentration risk, or does it help to diversify my investments?
Get Smart: Your First Investment Is Really a Lesson in Patience
Singapore investors have access to a wide range of investment opportunities, from local dividend stocks and REITs to global growth companies and ETFs.
There’s always the next correction, hot stock, and investment trend.
Rather than chasing trends, start early and understand what you own to stay invested through different market cycles and enjoy the power of
compounding
.
If the market falls further, will you be ready… or fully invested?

title: Australia raises key rate to 15-year high to cool inflation
article:
(Sept 29): Australia’s central bank resumed raising interest rates on Tuesday, judging it couldn’t wait any longer to respond to rising energy costs and resilient domestic demand that threaten to intensify inflationary pressures.

The Reserve Bank’s board lifted the cash rate to 4.6% from 4.35%, as widely expected, taking rates to the highest level in about 15 years. The nine-member policy committee voted unanimously to deliver its fourth hike this year, saying firms are experiencing cost pressures and either increasing prices or looking to do so.

“Since the previous meeting, some of the upside risks to inflation are materialising,” the policy board said in its statement. “The board will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target, including increasing the cash rate target further if needed.”

The Australian dollar fluctuated between a small gain and loss to hold above 70 US cents as investors digested the decision. Yields on policy-sensitive three-year notes trimmed an earlier decline to trade one basis point lower at 5.03%.

Traders lifted bets on a further RBA rate hike, with swaps pricing a 56% chance of a follow-up move in November. Prior to the decision, it was seen as roughly a coin toss.

See also: South Korea tax windfall seen above 50 tril won — Yonhap

The RBA joins counterparts in Europe, the US and Japan in raising rates this month to tackle escalating price pressures fueled by the US-Iran war. With little prospect of an early resolution to the conflict and energy prices surging across the global economy, central banks are having to act.

“November’s RBA meeting is live, particularly given today’s unanimous decision,” Katherine Palmer, head of fixed income strategy at BlackRock’s Australian unit wrote in a note. “Domestic capacity pressures continue, while elevated oil prices and geopolitical uncertainty have added to the risk that inflation remains persistent.”

RBA officials had sent increasingly hawkish signals in recent weeks and indicated a willingness to hike if needed to try to ensure inflation heads back to its 2%-3% target band. The central bank increased borrowing costs at its first three meetings of the year, worrying about building price pressures even before the energy shock unleashed by war in the Middle East.

See also: It’s time to reconsider inflation targeting

“Higher fuel prices have partially been passed through to prices of other goods and services. This inflation impulse is in addition to the effect of capacity pressures in the economy,” the statement said. “The board remains focused on ensuring that high inflation does not become embedded.”

The RBA stood pat at 4.35% at its past two meetings, trying to gauge the impact of its rapid-fire moves on the economy. Tuesday’s hike now takes cumulative tightening this year to 1 percentage point. The risk of a follow-up rate rise in November has also been widely discussed by economists due to the spectre of price pressures becoming entrenched.

The OECD has projected that inflation in wealthy nations will linger in 2027, warning central banks including Australia’s to “remain very vigilant” and intervene more than they did during the post-pandemic period. The International Monetary Fund sent a similar warning to the RBA directly this month, urging it to stand ready to hike.

Australia will release monthly inflation data for August on Wednesday, which is likely to be an important input for policymakers, though the RBA’s favoured quarterly report will be available before the next meeting in November.

The statement “delivers a consistent message of inflation concern, despite the three prior rate hikes, the slowdown in housing, and the slight easing in labour market strength”, said Sean Keane, chief strategist for Asia Pacific at JB Drax Honore. “This is a central bank that is clearly prepared to hike again this year, not because they want to, but quite simply because they may have to.”

Tuesday’s tightening is set to weigh further on Australia’s housing market, already in a downturn and with linkages across the economy. It may push unemployment higher after the jobless rate rose to 4.6% last month.

“In Australia, weak productivity growth continues to constrain potential growth and there are uncertainties about the economic effects of the downturn in the housing market,” the board said.

title: Toyota sales fall for seventh straight month on China slump
article:
(Sept 29): Toyota Motor Corp’s car sales fell again last month due to a prolonged slump in China, where legacy brands are grappling with mounting competition from fast-moving local electric-vehicle makers.

Toyota and Lexus brand sales cratered 23% in the world’s biggest auto market in August on weak demand for gasoline and hybrid vehicles, the Japanese manufacturer said Tuesday. That dragged down its global group deliveries, which declined 7.5% from a year earlier.

Toyota and its peers have been contending with a shrinking market in China, where consumers are shying away from expensive purchases due to an ongoing real estate crisis. Carmakers are also dealing with uneven demand for EVs, and soaring oil prices triggered by the fighting in the Middle East.

Honda Motor Co’s global sales fell 9.2% in August, dragged down by a 50% slump in China. Nissan Motor Co’s deliveries in the country plummeted 52%, resulting in a global sales decline of 17.5%.

Toyota and Lexus did better elsewhere, with sales rising 2.6% in Europe and 9.1% in Japan thanks to robust demand for new models, especially hybrids. They declined 4.4% in the US and fell by more than a third in the Middle East.

Earlier this year, Toyota said hybrid sales are on track to exceed five million units for the first time in 2026. Alternative powertrains have provided the Japanese carmaker with a strong arsenal in the US, where steep tariffs have all but blocked BYD Co and other Chinese brands from entering the market.

See also: Goldman's John Waldron edges closer to succeeding Solomon as CEO

title: AMD to buy Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs AI startup for US$8.2 bil
article:
(Sept 29): Chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices Inc agreed to acquire World Labs for US$8.2 billion ($10.48 billion), gaining an artificial intelligence (AI) startup founded by industry pioneer and researcher Fei-Fei Li.

The all-stock transaction is expected to close by the end of the year, subject to regulatory approvals, the companies said in a statement Monday.

AMD, a key challenger to Nvidia Corp in the market for AI chips, is adding a team of leading researchers and their models, along with insights into how the AI field is evolving. That should help the company plan its future hardware releases.

“The more you understand end to end, the better system you are going to build,” AMD chief executive officer Lisa Su said in a Bloomberg Television interview that’s slated to air on Monday afternoon.

“That’s why we are acquiring World Labs,” Su said. “To have access to the world-class talent Fei-Fei has brought together and bring it together with AMD’s capabilities around hardware, software and systems.”

World Labs develops so-called world models: AI software that can run applications in the physical world. The models generate and reconstruct three-dimensional environments, which the startup says can be used to help advance work on robots, scientific discovery and factory equipment.

See also: China may let Alibaba buy Nvidia’s RTX chips, Information reports

Li, who served as CEO of World Labs, is a renowned researcher and computer scientist at Stanford University. As part of the agreement, she will join AMD as an executive vice president and chief scientist and report directly to Su.

“As our company grows, so does our ambition,” Li said in the Bloomberg Television interview. And that has increased the startup’s need for computing power, she said.

“At this point, if we can join forces with AMD, we really are giving ourselves, AMD and the ecosystem an opportunity to accelerate the flywheel between software and hardware development,” she said.

See also: Bill Gates says Trump is wrong to hold out against AI safeguards

The deal will also help bolster AMD’s offerings by allowing it to provide a variety of AI models to customers. The company has been expanding its lineup in a bid to sell more products and services to data centre clients, its biggest source of revenue. The idea is to offer the necessary elements to rapidly set up the facilities and put them into operation.

“You are going to have both open as well as proprietary models,” Su said. “AMD has been a contributor there. I think we are going to expand that contribution.”

Ultimately, the goal is to build better AI, Su added. “Our ambition is to define the future of AI compute.”

AMD’s larger rival Nvidia pioneered the approach of bundling equipment and services with AI chips to help clients get up and running quickly. It’s now using the strategy to target new kinds of customers — going beyond the cloud computing giants that still fuel much of its growth.

Nvidia recently agreed to acquire another high-profile AI startup, Hugging Face, in a deal valued at about US$13 billion.

World Labs, launched in 2024, has about 70 employees. That includes a team of robotics experts from its July acquisition of SceniX, a startup that builds software to train robots in realistic virtual worlds.

During Su’s 12-year tenure as AMD’s leader, the chipmaker has sought to be recognised for its technical capabilities and escape its reputation as an also-ran in Silicon Valley. In the company’s core processor market, AMD has already emerged from the shadow of Intel Corp and now has products that are rated the best in the industry.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

In the market for AI accelerators — chips used to train and run AI models — AMD remains a distant second to Nvidia. But Su has rolled out new products that she says can outperform offerings from its larger rival.

Investors see the company as a key beneficiary of AI spending and have bid up its shares nearly threefold this year. That’s given AMD a valuation of roughly US$1 trillion, a distinction shared with only about a dozen other tech titans.

Nvidia remains the world’s most valuable company, with a market capitalisation above US$5 trillion. But its shares are only up about 22% this year, underperforming nearly all major chipmakers in 2026.

title: AI faces US$6 tril test to justify data centres, Bain says
article:
(Sept 29): The global AI industry needs to earn US$6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to justify the capital being deployed to build data centres around the world, Bain & Co said.

Existing consumer and enterprise AI services may generate as much as US$1.8 trillion of that sum, leaving US$4.2 trillion in new revenue that needs to be created, the consulting firm said Tuesday in its annual global technology report. The shortfall likely will come from nascent segments ranging from autonomous machines to robotics, as well as emerging fields such as drug discovery, mental health and energy generation, it said.

“What the industry needs is a wave of innovation that will dwarf what mobile and cloud unlocked,” said David Crawford, the report’s lead author and chairman of Bain’s Global Technology, Media, and Telecommunications practice. “AI infrastructure is being built well ahead of the demand curve and funding it sustainably will require adding approximately 1% to the annual global GDP growth rate,” he said.

Bain’s report highlights the hurdles ahead to make the current pace of AI development sustainable.

Companies led by Microsoft Corp, Alphabet Inc’s Google, Amazon.com Inc, Meta Platforms Inc and Oracle Corp are investing trillions of dollars in data centres to quench AI’s demand for computational resources. Data centre sizes and costs are doubling roughly every 12 to 16 months, in part due to surging prices of chips from the likes of Nvidia Corp and SK Hynix Inc, networking equipment and other components.

The report comes as debate intensifies around the as-yet elusive returns for AI service providers. Critics worry about an increasingly interconnected web of dependencies between technology manufacturers and AI developers that help to propel lofty expectations that in turn require bigger sums of money.

See also: Sony to skip CES show after Honda EV venture dropped

While discussions today are fixated on employee productivity, the economics of AI infrastructure will demand trillions in new revenue beyond productivity gains, Bain said.

The consultancy projects US$5 trillion to US$6.5 trillion of data-centre spending by 2030, adding at least 150 gigawatts of capacity that will further strain countries’ energy resources. Annual spending on AI infrastructure — spanning data centres, computing capacity and upgrades in accelerators and memory chips — may reach as much as US$1.5 trillion by 2031, it said.

Data center developers already face shortages in transformers and water and power supplies, as well as fierce local opposition that’s blocked or delayed US$68 billion worth of projects in the June quarter in the US.

title: MAS places $1.45 bil with five asset managers; reviewing proposals for a fourth batch of asset managers
article:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) announced today (Sept 29) the appointment of the third batch of five asset managers under the $6.5 billion Equity Market Development Programme (EQDP).

MAS will be placing a total of $1.45 billion with five appointed managers, which are, Amundi, Franklin Templeton, HSBC Asset Management, M&G Investments and Natixis Investment Managers.

With this latest $1.45 billion allocation, this will bring the total allocation under the EQDP to $5.4 billion.

At the same time, MAS has also committed $20 million from the Financial Sector Development Fund (FSDF) to the Grant for Equity Market Singapore (GEMS) Scheme to enhance equities market making activities in Singapore.

The grant will support appointed market makers in providing trading liquidity for an initial group of around 80 eligible small- and mid-cap stocks, as well as newly-listed stocks.

“It aims to facilitate tighter bid-ask spreads, reduce execution costs, and strengthen price discovery. The list of eligible stocks will be reviewed regularly to cover additional stocks that can benefit from enhanced market making support to improve price discovery,” MAS states.

See also: SGX RegCo rolls out enhanced disclosures to drive value creation

These announcements were made during the SuperReturn Asia Conference on Sept 29 by Mr Chee Hong Tat, Minister for National Development and Deputy Chairman of MAS.

Meanwhile, MAS is reviewing proposals for a fourth batch of asset managers, and expects to complete the review in 2027.

"We are excited to contribute to the continued development and internationalisation of Singapore’s equity market, building on HSBC’s longstanding commitment to Singapore and its asset management ecosystem," says Pang Qi Lim, CEO of HSBC Asset Management Singapore and Head of Strategic Partnerships for South East Asia.

See also: EQDP fund manager Eastspring Investments launches new Singapore Income and Growth Equity Fund

"Bringing together HSBC Asset Management’s investment capabilities and the bank’s deep institutional banking and wealth network, with both local and global reach – we are uniquely positioned to connect clients across markets to trade, invest, grow, and manage risk internationally," says Pang.

"We look forward to leveraging these strengths to attract capital, broaden investor participation to further support the growth of a more vibrant and internationally connected equity market," he adds.

title: Oil extends gain as Iran uncertainty outweighs Saudi pipe return
article:
(Sept 29): Oil rose for a second day as a lack of progress in US-Iran talks and signs of strong demand outweighed a resumption of flows through a key pipeline from top exporter Saudi Arabia.

Brent traded near US$107 a barrel after ticking higher in the previous session, while West Texas Intermediate headed toward US$94. Iranian officials have privately expressed pessimism about reaching a deal to end hostilities with Washington and reopen the Strait of Hormuz before US midterm elections in November, following US President Donald Trump’s rejection of a proposal to resume full traffic through the waterway in seven days.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia has restored about half the flows through its cross-country East-West pipeline, a crucial route bypassing the strait, after drone strikes halted operations earlier this month. Flows through the link to the Red Sea have reached at least 3.5 million barrels a day, according to people familiar with the matter.

“There’s still enormous geopolitical risk, but the market has learned that barrels keep finding a way out,” said Haris Khurshid, chief investment officer at Karobaar Capital LP. “We’re not seeing the kind of sustained repricing you’d expect if traders thought physical supply was about to deteriorate materially.”

Crude is headed for a third monthly gain on the escalating US-Iran tensions, disruptions to the Saudi bypass route and potential diesel export curbs by Washington. Brent is up more than 70% this year, after more than seven months of conflict in the Middle East.

Trump denied an Axios report that he offered Iran sanctions relief and the release of frozen funds in exchange for concrete steps on its nuclear programme. The Islamic Republic’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also refuted that Tehran was prepared to show flexibility on the nuclear issue, according to state news agency IRNA.

See also: Saudi Arabia’s key oil pipeline starts exports after repairs

Brent faces greater downside than upside risk, Khurshid said. A credible US-Iran deal would potentially shave as much as US$15 off prices, while US$120 a barrel would require an actual supply disruption, he added.

However, key gauges of supply tightness have spiked in recent days in a sign of a clamour for barrels that can be delivered quickly. Meanwhile, fuel prices are surging as global refinery capacity remains hobbled.

Brent’s prompt spread — the difference between its two nearest contracts — has widened to more than US$7 a barrel, from less than US$1 at the end of last month. The bullish pattern, known as backwardation, is a classic indicator of a tight market. In Europe, Dated Brent — a critical physical-market benchmark — has been trading at a wide premium to futures.

See also: Trump says he’s ‘very seriously’ looking at diesel export ban

Separately, TotalEnergies SE chief executive officer Patrick Pouyanné said a US ban on diesel exports being considered by Trump to curb high prices could backfire by pushing up gasoline costs. “It’s a bad idea” as it forces the nation’s refineries to cut throughput, potentially driving up domestic gasoline prices, he said.
• Brent for November settlement rose 1.4% to US$106.72 a barrel at 10.13am in Singapore.
• November futures expire on Wednesday. The more-active December contract advanced 1.5% to US$99.26 a barrel.

title: Goldman's John Waldron edges closer to succeeding Solomon as CEO
article:
(Sept 29): A year after Goldman Sachs Group Inc’s board offered John Waldron US$80 million to stay for the top job, it’s moving to ensure he doesn’t wait too long.

The board has discussed a plan where Waldron, who is currently chief operating officer, would succeed David Solomon as CEO as early as next year, the Wall Street Journal reported.

It’s becoming more apparent that Waldron, 57, long seen as the likely successor, is nearing the final step in his rise to the top of Goldman. Last year, the board telegraphed its view of Waldron’s future when it gave him a restricted stock package now worth nearly US$120 million to stay five more years — matching the incentive given to Solomon.

But the timing has remained unclear. Solomon, 64, has been in the job for eight years. And while his early-tenure push into the consumer business faltered, the bank’s been riding high in the years since, with its equity-trading desk hitting record after record and its investment bankers reeling in the highest fees since 2021.

With the latest plan, Waldron could take over toward the end of 2027 or in 2028, the Journal said, citing people familiar with the matter whom it didn’t identify. Solomon would likely become executive chairman for about one or two years after he steps down as CEO.

“Of course the board regularly discusses succession, as we disclose in our filings, but there is no definitive timeline for succession at Goldman Sachs,” Tony Fratto, a bank spokesman, said in an emailed statement. “Any assertions about timing are just speculation.”

See also: South Korea’s three-year yield rises to highest level since 2022

Waldron, who is also Goldman’s president, joined the bank back in 2000 and has steadily risen. He ran the media and entertainment banking group before becoming a head of leveraged finance.

He’s also worked closely with Solomon throughout his career. In 2014, Waldron was elevated to head the investment bank alongside Solomon and Richard Gnodde.

When Solomon was named CEO in 2018, he tapped Waldron for the coveted second-most important position at the bank.

See also: Rising fuel costs drive up brewing costs in Asia, Heineken says

“We are a close-knit group, who grew up together in the firm,” Waldron said at the bank’s investor day in 2020. “We now have a unique opportunity to lead this great institution forward.”

As president, Waldron has overseen key initiatives at Goldman to spur collaboration across the firm and drive gains from efficiency in artificial intelligence. He’s also pushed to grow the firm’s footprint outside of major financial hubs worldwide, helping cut costs and expand its talent pool.

In an CNBC interview in May, he described Goldman as a “human assembly line” that was ripe for automation from AI.

“Our human assembly lines will become more digitised, digital agents will be our robots,” Waldron said. “I’m not sure dynamically how the overall headcount will change, but I think the firm is going to get much more resilient and much more scalable.”

title: Mapletree Industrial Trust to divest 3255 Neil Armstrong Boulevard at US$9.8 mil, 10% below independent valuation
article:
Mapletree Industrial Trust (MIT) announced that it has entered into a sales and purchase agreement for the divestment of 3255 Neil Armstrong Boulevard, located in the US to DataBank Properties, LLC, which is the current tenant of the property, for a total consideration of US$9.81 million ($12.54 million).

The property is a single-storey building with a net lettable area of about 87,402 sq ft and is sited on freehold land with a land area of about 343,253 sq ft.

The manager states that the sale price was determined pursuant to the pricing mechanism set out in the lease agreement. While the sale price represents a 9% premium above MIT’s purchase price of US$9.0 million, it is 10% below the independent valuation of US$10.9 million as at March 31.

The property contributed about 0.2% to MIT’s portfolio gross revenue in the financial year ended March 31.

The manager expects the proposed divestment to be completed by the fourth quarter of 2026 and the net proceeds may be used to pare down debts and fund working capital requirements.

As at 9.41am, Units in MIT was trading 1 cent lower, or down 0.53% at $1.86.

title: Treasuries stabilise after sell-off, stocks slip
article:
(Sept 29): Bond investors got a respite in early Asian trading from a bruising sell-off after surging oil prices and mounting bets on further Federal Reserve (Fed) interest-rate hikes drove Treasury yields to multi-year highs. Asian stocks fell.

The US 10-year yield was little changed at 5.23% after climbing as much as 11 basis points on Monday to the highest since 2007. Two- and 30-year yields were also little changed as traders braced for the Fed to keep tightening policy to rein in inflation. Australian government bonds held steady before a central bank monetary policy decision later Tuesday.

Brent crude advanced for a second day, climbing 1.1% to US$106.44 a barrel, as optimism for an imminent diplomatic breakthrough in the Middle East faded. Gold was little changed around US$4,118 an ounce after slumping almost 4% on Monday.

MSCI’s Asia Pacific share index declined 0.3%, with losses in South Korea and Japan. Equity-index futures for Wall Street benchmarks slipped 0.1%.

Climbing oil prices have weighed on global bond markets by keeping inflation risks alive and reinforcing expectations that interest rates will stay higher for longer. In the US, stronger business activity and concerns over elevated government debt levels have fuelled the biggest Treasury sell-off since US President Donald Trump’s April 2025 tariff rollout rattled markets.

“The broader market hasn’t been able to gain much traction because of rising yields and oil prices,” said Chris Larkin at E*Trade from Morgan Stanley. “With the Fed focused on the inflation side of its mandate, unless this week’s labour-market data is a major surprise, it will likely play second fiddle to interest rates and energy.”

See also: Bonds drop with stocks as Iran tensions boost oil

Iran and the US remained far apart on a ceasefire and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran sticking to a proposal Trump has rejected. Trump denied an Axios report that he’s willing to offer sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian funds in exchange “for concrete nuclear concessions”.

Iranian officials have privately expressed pessimism about reaching an agreement to end hostilities and reopen the strait before the US midterm elections in November, according to people familiar with the matter.

“Our expectations remain that the conflict will be with markets for the foreseeable future and the global economy will continue adjusting to the realities of the supply disruptions,” said Ian Lyngen at BMO Capital Markets.

See also: House of cards in bonds

Investors will also be watching a packed slate of US economic data this week for signs the economy remains strong enough to support further Fed tightening. Consumer confidence and August JOLTS figures are due Tuesday, followed by consumer-spending and inflation data and then payrolls on Friday.

“If economic resilience and investment demand remain intact, there may still be scope for yields to move higher,” said Seema Shah at Principal Asset Management.
• The board of Goldman Sachs has discussed a plan for David Solomon to step down as chief executive and be replaced with chief operating officer John Waldron as soon as next year, according to people familiar with the matter.
• Anthropic reported a net loss of US$42 billion in 2025, and plans to spend US$518 billion on cloud, computing and infrastructure obligations in the coming years, Reuters reported, citing its IPO prospectus.
• OpenAI cancelled plans to release its latest artificial intelligence model after researchers discovered safety risks during testing, according to the Wall Street Journal.
• Chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices Inc agreed to acquire World Labs for US$8.2 billion, gaining an artificial intelligence startup founded by industry pioneer and researcher Fei-Fei Li.
